---

## The researcher's workflow problem

Most survey studies lose time and rigour at every handoff point.

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
**The typical path today**

1. Design questions in Word or a web form
2. Deploy to a third-party platform
3. Export a spreadsheet
4. Decide which tests to run *after seeing the data*
5. Write up results manually
:::
::: {.col}
**What goes wrong**

- The link between questions and constructs exists only in the researcher's head
- Analysis decisions made after viewing data introduce bias
- Reproducing the study means re-reading a PDF, not re-running code
- Quality checks are manual — or skipped
:::
:::

::: {.callout-amber}
**The core problem:** there is no machine-readable contract between the instrument, the analysis plan, and the data.
:::

---

## surveyframe solves this in five steps

::: {.workflow}
::: {.wf-step}
Design
:::
::: {.wf-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.wf-step}
Deploy
:::
::: {.wf-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.wf-step}
Collect
:::
::: {.wf-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.wf-step}
Analyse
:::
::: {.wf-arrow}
→
:::
::: {.wf-step}
Report
:::
:::

Each step is one R function call. The instrument is a typed R object that carries the analysis plan, the measurement model, and the quality rules — declared before any data is collected.

::: {.callout}
**The key idea:** analysis is the *execution* of a pre-declared plan, not a post-hoc search. The instrument is a methodological contract.
:::

---

## What you can do with surveyframe

::: {.feature-grid}
::: {.feature-card}
**🏗️ Build**

Design in R code or the visual GUI. 11 item types, skip logic, attention checks, measurement models.
:::
::: {.feature-card}
**🚀 Deploy**

Export a self-contained offline HTML survey. No server. Standard or conversational presentation mode.
:::
::: {.feature-card}
**📊 Analyse**

Pre-declared analysis plan with one call. 20+ statistical methods. APA-formatted results and writing prompts.
:::
::: {.feature-card}
**🔒 Integrity**

Every `.sframe` file carries a SHA-256 hash. Tampering is caught immediately on `read_sframe()`.
:::
::: {.feature-card}
**📋 Report**

APA-formatted HTML reports: codebook, quality summary, descriptives, reliability, analysis results.
:::
::: {.feature-card}
**📦 Reproduce**

The full workflow is R code. Any collaborator re-runs it from scratch — no clicks to remember.
:::
:::

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Part 1 — Design your instrument</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Components, item types, scales, logic, and models</p>
:::

---

## The five building blocks

Every surveyframe instrument is assembled from five component types.

| Component | Function | What it defines |
|---|---|---|
| Choice set | `sf_choices()` | The labelled response options |
| Item | `sf_item()` | One question and its response type |
| Scale | `sf_scale()` | A group of items scored together |
| Branch rule | `sf_branch()` | Skip logic — show or hide based on response |
| Quality check | `sf_check()` | Attention, timing, or pattern rules |

```r
# Assemble all components into one validated object
instr <- sf_instrument(
  title      = "Tourism Services Survey",
  version    = "1.0.0",
  authors    = "Mohammed Ali Sharafuddin",
  components = list(agree5, sat_1, sat_2, sat_scale, branch_1, attn_check)
)
```

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Item types</p>
<p class="chap-sub">11 response formats — one slide each</p>
:::

---

## Item type 1 — Likert

Horizontal radio buttons. One column per option, label centred below.
Use a choice set with a defined number of points.

```r
agree5 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "agree5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral",
             "Agree", "Strongly agree")
)

sat_1 <- sf_item(
  id         = "sat_1",
  label      = "The service met my expectations.",
  type       = "likert",
  choice_set = "agree5",
  scale_id   = "satisfaction",
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Likert items store numeric values (1–5 or 1–7). The labels are display-only. Reverse scoring is declared with `reverse = TRUE` in `sf_item()`.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: 5-point Likert rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 1 continued — 7-point Likert

The same `type = "likert"` — change the choice set to 7 points.

```r
agree7 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "agree7",
  values = 1:7,
  labels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree",
             "Somewhat disagree", "Neutral",
             "Somewhat agree", "Agree", "Strongly agree")
)

sq_1 <- sf_item(
  id         = "sq_1",
  label      = "Staff were helpful and professional.",
  type       = "likert",
  choice_set = "agree7",
  scale_id   = "service_quality",
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Any number of points is supported. Common scales: 5-point, 7-point, 4-point (no neutral), 6-point (no neutral + more granularity).
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: 7-point Likert rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 2 — Single choice

Vertical radio buttons. One option can be selected.
Use when the response options are not a numeric continuum.

```r
visit_purpose <- sf_choices(
  id     = "purpose",
  values = c("leisure", "business", "education", "family"),
  labels = c("Leisure", "Business", "Education", "Family visit")
)

q_purpose <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_purpose",
  label      = "What was the primary purpose of your visit?",
  type       = "single_choice",
  choice_set = "purpose",
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
`single_choice` stores the chosen value string. `likert` stores an integer. Use `single_choice` for categorical questions; use `likert` for ordered scales.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: single_choice rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 3 — Multiple choice

Checkboxes. Any number of options can be selected.
Stored as a comma-separated string of chosen values.

```r
channels <- sf_choices(
  id     = "channels",
  values = c("instagram", "facebook", "tiktok", "word_of_mouth", "travel_agent"),
  labels = c("Instagram", "Facebook", "TikTok",
             "Word of mouth", "Travel agent")
)

q_channels <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_channels",
  label      = "Which channels influenced your booking decision? (select all that apply)",
  type       = "multiple_choice",
  choice_set = "channels",
  required   = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout}
`multiple_choice` supports a `min_selections` and `max_selections` argument in `sf_item()` to constrain the number of selections.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: multiple_choice (checkboxes) rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 4 — Numeric input

A validated number entry field. Accepts integer or decimal values.
Use for age, count, spending, or any continuous numeric response.

```r
q_age <- sf_item(
  id       = "q_age",
  label    = "What is your age?",
  type     = "numeric",
  required = TRUE
)

q_spend <- sf_item(
  id          = "q_spend",
  label       = "Approximately how much did you spend (USD)?",
  type        = "numeric",
  required    = FALSE,
  placeholder = "Enter amount"
)
```

::: {.callout}
Non-numeric characters are rejected in the browser. The value is stored as a number. Use `slider` instead when you want to constrain the range visually.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: numeric input rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 5 — Short text

A single-line free-text field.
Use for names, brief labels, or any open short-form answer.

```r
q_name <- sf_item(
  id          = "q_name",
  label       = "What is your first name? (optional)",
  type        = "text",
  required    = FALSE,
  placeholder = "Your name"
)

q_country <- sf_item(
  id          = "q_country",
  label       = "Which country are you from?",
  type        = "text",
  required    = TRUE,
  placeholder = "Country of residence"
)
```

::: {.callout}
`text` renders as `<input type="text">`. For longer answers (multiple sentences), use `textarea` instead.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: short text input rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 6 — Long text (textarea)

A multi-line free-text area.
Use for open-ended feedback, comments, or any qualitative response.

```r
q_feedback <- sf_item(
  id          = "q_feedback",
  label       = "Please share any additional comments or suggestions.",
  type        = "textarea",
  required    = FALSE,
  placeholder = "Write your response here…"
)

q_improve <- sf_item(
  id       = "q_improve",
  label    = "What could we improve about your experience?",
  type     = "textarea",
  required = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Textarea responses are stored as plain character strings. They are excluded from scale scoring and psychometric analysis automatically.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: textarea rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 7 — Date

A date picker field. Stored as YYYY-MM-DD.
Use for visit dates, event dates, or date-of-birth.

```r
q_visit_date <- sf_item(
  id       = "q_visit_date",
  label    = "When did your visit take place?",
  type     = "date",
  required = TRUE
)

q_dob <- sf_item(
  id       = "q_dob",
  label    = "Date of birth (optional)",
  type     = "date",
  required = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout}
The browser renders a native date picker. The value is validated as a real date before the respondent can proceed. Stored in the CSV as `YYYY-MM-DD`.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: date picker rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 8 — Slider

A horizontal draggable slider. Define min, max, and step.
Use for willingness-to-pay, percentage confidence, or any bounded continuous scale.

```r
q_wtp <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_wtp",
  label      = "How much would you be willing to pay for this experience? (USD)",
  type       = "slider",
  slider_min = 0,
  slider_max = 500,
  slider_step = 10,
  required   = TRUE
)

q_conf <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_conf",
  label      = "How confident are you in your answer? (0 = not at all, 100 = completely)",
  type       = "slider",
  slider_min = 0,
  slider_max = 100,
  slider_step = 1,
  required   = TRUE
)
```

<!-- SCREENSHOT: slider rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 9 — Star rating

A clickable star or numeric rating.
Use for overall satisfaction, recommendation likelihood, or product scores.

```r
q_overall <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_overall",
  label      = "Overall, how would you rate your experience?",
  type       = "rating",
  rating_max = 5,
  required   = TRUE
)

q_recommend <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_recommend",
  label      = "How likely are you to recommend this destination?",
  type       = "rating",
  rating_max = 10,
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
`rating_max` sets the number of stars or points. Values are stored as integers (1 to `rating_max`). Compatible with scale scoring and reliability analysis.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: star rating rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 10 — Matrix / rating grid

A grid of Likert rows sharing the same column headers.
Use for attribute evaluation, service quality batteries, or importance-performance grids.

```r
# Column headers defined in the choice set
perf_choices <- sf_choices(
  id     = "perf5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Very poor", "Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent")
)

q_matrix <- sf_item(
  id           = "q_hotel",
  label        = "Rate the following aspects of your hotel stay:",
  type         = "matrix",
  choice_set   = "perf5",
  matrix_items = c("Room cleanliness", "Staff friendliness",
                   "Value for money", "Location", "Breakfast quality"),
  required     = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Each matrix row becomes a separate variable in the data (e.g., `q_hotel_1`, `q_hotel_2`, …). Assign them to a scale for composite scoring.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: matrix grid rendered in the survey -->

---

## Item type 11 — Rank order

Drag-and-drop ranking. Respondents sort options from most to least preferred.
Use for priority-setting, feature preference, or destination ranking.

```r
rank_choices <- sf_choices(
  id     = "destinations",
  values = c("bali", "dubai", "paris", "singapore", "tokyo"),
  labels = c("Bali", "Dubai", "Paris", "Singapore", "Tokyo")
)

q_rank <- sf_item(
  id         = "q_rank",
  label      = "Rank these destinations from most preferred (1) to least preferred (5).",
  type       = "ranking",
  choice_set = "destinations",
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Stored as rank integers in the data (1 = most preferred). Use `kruskal_wallis` or `friedman` in your analysis plan when comparing ranked responses across groups.
:::

<!-- SCREENSHOT: ranking drag-and-drop rendered in the survey -->

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Choice sets</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Define once, reuse across all items</p>
:::

---

## Choice sets — 5-point agree-disagree

The most common choice set in survey research.
Define once with `sf_choices()`, reference by id in every item that uses it.

```r
agree5 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "agree5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral",
             "Agree", "Strongly agree")
)
```

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
**Used for:** satisfaction, service quality, attitude, agreement, importance, perception scales.

**Scoring:** values 1–5 are numeric. `score_scales()` averages them (or sums with `method = "sum"`).
:::
::: {.col}
**With reverse scoring:**
```r
# Item scored from highest to lowest
sat_neg <- sf_item(
  id         = "sat_neg",
  label      = "I was disappointed overall.",
  type       = "likert",
  choice_set = "agree5",
  reverse    = TRUE,
  scale_id   = "satisfaction"
)
```
:::
:::

---

## Choice sets — 7-point agree-disagree

More granularity. Reduces ceiling and floor effects.
Recommended for attitude measurement when sample size allows it.

```r
agree7 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "agree7",
  values = 1:7,
  labels = c("Strongly disagree", "Disagree",
             "Somewhat disagree", "Neutral",
             "Somewhat agree", "Agree", "Strongly agree")
)

# Or: a 7-point importance scale
import7 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "import7",
  values = 1:7,
  labels = c("Not at all important", "Slightly important",
             "Somewhat important", "Moderately important",
             "Important", "Very important", "Extremely important")
)
```

::: {.callout}
A 7-point scale tends to produce distributions closer to normal than a 5-point scale, which can improve the fit of CFA models. Use it when constructs require fine-grained discrimination.
:::

---

## Choice sets — frequency, satisfaction, quality

Built-in named scales for common constructs.

```r
# Frequency
freq5 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "freq5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Never", "Rarely", "Sometimes", "Often", "Always")
)

# Satisfaction
sat5 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "sat5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Very dissatisfied", "Dissatisfied", "Neutral",
             "Satisfied", "Very satisfied")
)

# Quality
qual5 <- sf_choices(
  id     = "qual5",
  values = 1:5,
  labels = c("Very poor", "Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Excellent")
)
```

::: {.callout}
Define choice sets once in your instrument and share them across items. All items referencing `"agree5"` show identical options — ensuring consistency and reducing object count.
:::

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Scales</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Group items, declare scoring, enable psychometrics</p>
:::

---

## Scales — mean scoring

A scale groups a set of items and scores them together.
`method = "mean"` (the default) averages the item values.

```r
sat_scale <- sf_scale(
  id     = "satisfaction",
  label  = "Tourist Satisfaction",
  items  = c("sat_1", "sat_2", "sat_3"),
  method = "mean"
)

# After scoring: one column per scale in your data frame
scored <- score_scales(responses, instr)
# scored$satisfaction = mean of sat_1, sat_2, sat_3 (per respondent)
```

::: {.callout}
Mean-scored scales are the standard for composite constructs in tourism, hospitality, and social science. The scale score becomes the input to `run_analysis_plan()` — no manual column creation needed.
:::

---

## Scales — sum scoring and reverse coding

`method = "sum"` adds item values instead of averaging.
Reverse-scored items are flipped automatically before scoring.

```r
# Sum-scored scale (e.g., symptom counts)
symptom_scale <- sf_scale(
  id     = "anxiety",
  label  = "Anxiety Symptoms",
  items  = c("anx_1", "anx_2", "anx_3", "anx_4"),
  method = "sum"
)

# Item declared as reverse-scored
anx_pos <- sf_item(
  id         = "anx_4",
  label      = "I feel calm and at ease.",
  type       = "likert",
  choice_set = "agree5",
  scale_id   = "anxiety",
  reverse    = TRUE      # 5 becomes 1, 4 becomes 2, etc.
)
```

::: {.callout}
`reverse = TRUE` on an item and the scale's `values` range are all surveyframe needs to flip the score. You do not write the reversal logic yourself.
:::

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Skip logic and quality checks</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Branches, attention items, timing rules</p>
:::

---

## Branch rules — conditional skip logic

`sf_branch()` shows or hides an item based on a previous answer.
Supports all comparison operators: `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`.

```r
# Show follow-up only if respondent rated 4 or 5
br_followup <- sf_branch(
  item_id    = "q_followup",   # item to show/hide
  depends_on = "q_overall",    # item whose value is checked
  operator   = ">=",
  value      = 4,
  action     = "show"          # "show" or "hide"
)

# Hide a complaint item if experience was positive
br_complaint <- sf_branch(
  item_id    = "q_complaint",
  depends_on = "q_overall",
  operator   = "<",
  value      = 3,
  action     = "show"
)
```

::: {.callout}
Branch targets that are hidden contribute no data. `read_responses()` marks them as `NA` automatically and flags them in the missing data report.
:::

---

## Quality checks — attention item

An attention check presents a deliberately obvious question.
Respondents who fail are flagged in the quality report.

```r
# A foil item: the "correct" answer is declared
attn_check <- sf_check(
  id          = "attn_1",
  item_id     = "attn_q",
  type        = "attention",
  pass_values = 4,     # only value 4 is correct
  fail_action = "flag" # flag but do not exclude automatically
)

# The item itself is a regular Likert item
attn_item <- sf_item(
  id         = "attn_q",
  label      = "Please select 'Agree' for this question to confirm you are reading carefully.",
  type       = "likert",
  choice_set = "agree5",
  required   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
`fail_action = "flag"` adds the respondent to the `flagged` list in `quality_report()`. Use `"exclude"` to drop flagged respondents automatically from `score_scales()`.
:::

---

## Quality checks — timing

A timing check flags respondents who complete too quickly.
The threshold is declared before data collection.

```r
timing_check <- sf_check(
  id          = "timing_1",
  type        = "timing",
  min_seconds = 120,    # flag if completed in under 2 minutes
  fail_action = "flag"
)
```

::: {.r-out}
── Quality report ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Respondents: 60   Flagged: 4   Flag rate: 6.7%

  Attention checks
    attn_q  pass: 56  fail: 4  pass rate: 93.3%

  Timing
    Median completion time: 312 s
    Fast completions (under 120 s): 0

  Missing data
    Items with any missing: 0
:::

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Measurement model</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Declare the structural model before analysis</p>
:::

---

## sf_model() — measurement model declaration

Declare latent factors, their indicators, and structural paths before fitting.
`sf_model()` stores the model inside the instrument — not in a separate script.

```r
cfa_model <- sf_model(
  type    = "cfa",
  factors = list(
    satisfaction          = c("sat_1", "sat_2", "sat_3"),
    service_quality       = c("sq_1",  "sq_2",  "sq_3"),
    behavioural_intention = c("bi_1",  "bi_2")
  )
)

sem_model <- sf_model(
  type    = "sem",
  factors = list(
    service_quality       = c("sq_1", "sq_2", "sq_3"),
    satisfaction          = c("sat_1", "sat_2"),
    behavioural_intention = c("bi_1",  "bi_2")
  ),
  paths   = list(
    c("service_quality", "satisfaction"),
    c("satisfaction",    "behavioural_intention")
  )
)
```

::: {.callout}
The model is stored in the instrument. `cfa_lavaan_syntax()` and `seminr_syntax()` generate ready-to-run code from it — no manual transcription of factor names.
:::

---

## Assemble and validate the instrument

`sf_instrument()` takes all components and validates them in one call.

```r
instr <- sf_instrument(
  title      = "Tourism Services Survey",
  version    = "1.0.0",
  authors    = "Mohammed Ali Sharafuddin",
  components = list(
    agree5, agree7, sat5,           # choice sets
    sat_1, sat_2, sat_3,            # items
    sq_1, sq_2, sq_3,               # more items
    bi_1, bi_2,                     # items
    attn_item,                      # attention check item
    sat_scale, sq_scale, bi_scale,  # scales
    br_followup,                    # branch rule
    attn_check, timing_check,       # quality checks
    cfa_model                       # measurement model
  )
)
print(instr)
```

::: {.r-out}
── surveyframe instrument ───────────────────────────────────────
  Title:   Tourism Services Survey  v1.0.0
  Items:   11   Scales: 3   Checks: 2   Branches: 1
  Model:   CFA   Factors: 3
  Status:  valid
:::

---

## Save and reload — SHA-256 integrity

`.sframe` files carry a cryptographic hash.
Re-loading the file after any change raises an error immediately.

```r
# Save
write_sframe(instr, "tourism_survey.sframe")

# Reload — hash is verified automatically
instr2 <- read_sframe("tourism_survey.sframe")

# If the file was tampered with:
# Error: SHA-256 hash mismatch.
# Expected: a3f9...  Got: 7b2c...
# The instrument file may have been altered after saving.
```

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout}
**Why this matters:** preregistration requires that the declared instrument is the one used in analysis. The hash proves the instrument was not changed after data collection began.
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-amber}
Never edit a `.sframe` file in a text editor. Always modify in R and call `write_sframe()` again. The old hash is invalidated and a new one is computed.
:::
:::
:::

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Part 2 — The GUI Builder</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Design visually, export as R code or .sframe</p>

## Export — Standard presentation mode

All items grouped by page. Respondents use Next and Back to navigate.

```r
export_static_survey(
  instr,
  output_path = "tourism_survey.html",
  open        = TRUE,
  overwrite   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Static survey written to 'tourism_survey.html' (184.6 KB).
:::

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-green}
**One file.** The complete survey — questions, logic, styling, and response capture — is a single HTML file you can email, share via QR code, or put on a USB stick. No internet connection needed.
:::
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout-green}
**Responses download as CSV** when the respondent clicks Submit. One file per respondent, or collect and merge with `read_responses()`.
:::
:::

---

## Export — Conversational presentation mode

One item per screen. Auto-advances on selection for Likert and single-choice items.

```r
instr$render$mode <- "conversational"

export_static_survey(
  instr,
  output_path = "tourism_survey_conv.html",
  open        = TRUE,
  overwrite   = TRUE
)
```

::: {.callout}
Conversational mode reduces perceived survey length and improves engagement for mobile respondents. The same item declarations, choice sets, and scale assignments are used — only the presentation changes.
:::

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Part 4 — Collect</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Read responses, run quality checks, flag problems</p>
:::

---

## Read responses

```r
# Load the bundled tourism demo
demo      <- sframe_demo_data()
instr_d   <- demo$instrument
responses <- demo$responses

cat("Items:    ", length(instr_d$items),  "\n")
cat("Scales:   ", length(instr_d$scales), "\n")
cat("Responses:", nrow(responses),        "\n")
```

::: {.r-out}
Items:     46
Scales:     9
Responses: 60
:::

```r
# Or read CSVs exported from the static survey
responses <- read_responses(
  "tourism_responses.csv",
  instr_d,
  respondent_id = "respondent_id",
  submitted_at  = "submitted_at",
  meta_cols     = "started_at"
)
```

::: {.callout}
`read_responses()` matches CSV columns to item ids, validates types, attaches timestamps, and returns a clean data frame. Unknown columns are ignored safely.
:::

---

## Quality report — attention and timing

```r
quality <- quality_report(
  responses, instr_d,
  respondent_id = "respondent_id",
  submitted_at  = "submitted_at",
  started_at    = "started_at"
)
print(quality)
```

::: {.r-out}
── Quality report ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Respondents: 60   Flagged: 4   Flag rate: 6.7%

  Attention checks
    attn_q  pass: 56  fail: 4  pass rate: 93.3%

  Timing
    Median completion time: 312 s
    Fast completions (under 60 s): 0

  Missing data
    Items with any missing: 0
:::

::: {.callout-amber}
Quality checks are **pre-declared in the instrument** via `sf_check()`. They run automatically from the instrument definition — nothing to configure at the analysis stage.
:::

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Part 5 — Analyse</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Score scales, run psychometrics, execute the analysis plan</p>
:::

---

## Score your scales

```r
scored <- score_scales(responses, instr_d)

# Scale summary
scale_cols <- c("digital_marketing", "service_quality",
                "sustainability", "satisfaction", "behavioural_intention")
data.frame(
  Scale = scale_cols,
  Mean  = round(colMeans(scored[, scale_cols], na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  SD    = round(apply(scored[, scale_cols], 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

::: {.r-out}
                Scale Mean   SD
1    digital_marketing 3.61 0.52
2      service_quality 3.80 0.44
3       sustainability 3.72 0.47
4         satisfaction 3.75 0.49
5 behavioural_intention 3.70 0.53
:::

::: {.callout}
`score_scales()` computes the mean or sum for each scale's items. Reverse-scored items are flipped automatically from the `reverse = TRUE` declaration in `sf_item()`.
:::

---

## Reliability — Cronbach's alpha

```r
rr <- reliability_report(scored, instr_d)
print(rr)
```

::: {.r-out}
── Reliability report ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  scale                  n_items  alpha  interpretation
  digital_marketing            3  0.884  Good
  service_quality              3  0.901  Excellent
  sustainability               2  0.856  Good
  satisfaction                 2  0.912  Excellent
  behavioural_intention        2  0.879  Good
:::

::: {.callout}
Alpha ≥ 0.70 = Acceptable · ≥ 0.80 = Good · ≥ 0.90 = Excellent (George & Mallery, 2003). The report runs on every scale declared in the instrument — no manual selection needed.
:::

---

## EFA readiness

```r
# Requires the psych package
er <- efa_report(scored, instr_d)
print(er)
```

::: {.r-out}
── EFA readiness ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  KMO overall: 0.87   Interpretation: Meritorious (Kaiser, 1974)
  Bartlett's test: χ²(10) = 147.3, p < .001  (factoring is appropriate)

  Per-item KMO:
    digital_marketing  0.88   service_quality  0.85   sustainability  0.91
    satisfaction       0.86   behavioural_intention  0.87

  Parallel analysis — suggested number of factors: 3
:::

::: {.callout}
KMO > 0.80 and a significant Bartlett test are the two standard requirements before running EFA. Both are checked and interpreted automatically.
:::

---

## Construct validity

```r
vr <- validity_report(
  list(
    satisfaction          = c(sat_1 = 0.84, sat_2 = 0.88),
    behavioural_intention = c(bi_1  = 0.81, bi_2  = 0.83)
  )
)
print(vr)
```

::: {.r-out}
── Validity report ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Construct             CR     AVE    Convergent   Discriminant
  satisfaction         0.905  0.726  Good (>0.50)  —
  behavioural_intention 0.877  0.681  Good (>0.50)  —

  AVE > shared variance with all other constructs: YES
:::

::: {.callout}
CR > 0.70 and AVE > 0.50 confirm convergent validity (Hair et al., 2019). AVE > maximum shared squared correlation confirms discriminant validity (Fornell-Larcker criterion).
:::

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">Analysis plan methods</p>
<p class="chap-sub">20+ statistical tests — declared before data collection</p>
:::

---

## Declare a research question

```r
rq1 <- sf_research_question(
  id        = "rq1",
  question  = "Is perceived digital marketing effectiveness associated with tourist satisfaction?",
  method    = "correlation_pearson",
  variables = list(x = "digital_marketing", y = "satisfaction")
)

# Multiple research questions collected in one plan
plan <- sf_analysis_plan(rq1, rq2, rq3)

# Or declare directly in sf_instrument() components list
instr <- sf_instrument(
  title      = "Tourism Survey",
  version    = "1.0.0",
  components = list(..., plan)
)
```

::: {.callout}
Research questions are declared before data collection. `run_analysis_plan()` executes every declared question and returns APA results and writing prompts. No test selection happens after seeing the data.
:::

---

## Pearson correlation

```r
# Declare
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "correlation_pearson",
  variables = list(x = "digital_marketing", y = "satisfaction")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   r(58) = .43, p = .001, 95% CI [.19, .62]
Effect:   Medium (Cohen, 1988)
Prompt:   There was a statistically significant positive relationship between
          digital marketing effectiveness and tourist satisfaction,
          r(58) = .43, p = .001, 95% CI [.19, .62].
:::

::: {.callout}
Assumes: bivariate normality, no extreme outliers. The output includes the test statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, effect size, and a citation-ready writing prompt.
:::

---

## Spearman correlation

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "correlation_spearman",
  variables = list(x = "ranking_score", y = "satisfaction")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   r_s(58) = .38, p = .003
Prompt:   A Spearman rank-order correlation indicated a statistically
          significant positive relationship between ranking score
          and satisfaction, r_s(58) = .38, p = .003.
:::

::: {.callout}
Use Spearman when variables are ordinal or when Pearson assumptions (normality) are not met. Operates on ranked values. No additional packages required.
:::

---

## Kendall's tau correlation

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "correlation_kendall",
  variables = list(x = "ranking_q", y = "preference_q")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   tau = .31, p = .014
Prompt:   Kendall's tau indicated a statistically significant positive
          association between ranking and preference, tau = .31, p = .014.
:::

::: {.callout}
Kendall's tau is more robust than Spearman for small samples or data with many tied ranks. Recommended when comparing ranked responses (use `ranking` item type as input).
:::

---

## Independent samples t-test

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "t_test_ind",
  question  = "Does satisfaction differ between first-time and repeat visitors?",
  variables = list(outcome = "satisfaction", group = "visit_type")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   t(58) = 2.14, p = .037, d = 0.55
Prompt:   An independent samples t-test indicated that satisfaction was
          significantly higher for first-time visitors (M = 3.91, SD = 0.48)
          than repeat visitors (M = 3.59, SD = 0.51), t(58) = 2.14,
          p = .037, d = 0.55.
:::

::: {.callout}
Levene's test is run automatically. If variances are unequal, Welch's correction is applied. Cohen's d is reported as the effect size.
:::

---

## Paired t-test

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "t_test_pair",
  question  = "Did expectations differ from actual experience?",
  variables = list(before = "expectation_score", after = "satisfaction")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   t(59) = -1.83, p = .072, d = 0.24
Prompt:   A paired samples t-test indicated no significant difference
          between expectation scores (M = 3.90, SD = 0.41) and actual
          satisfaction (M = 3.75, SD = 0.49), t(59) = -1.83, p = .072,
          d = 0.24.
:::

::: {.callout}
Use paired t-test when the same respondent provides both measurements (before/after, expectation/perception). The `before` and `after` variable roles are declared in the research question.
:::

---

## Mann-Whitney U

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "mann_whitney",
  question  = "Does satisfaction differ by visitor type (non-parametric)?",
  variables = list(outcome = "satisfaction", group = "visit_type")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   W = 512.0, p = .041, r = .26
Prompt:   A Mann-Whitney U test indicated a statistically significant
          difference in satisfaction between first-time and repeat visitors,
          W = 512.0, p = .041, r = .26 (small to medium effect).
:::

::: {.callout}
Use Mann-Whitney when the dependent variable is ordinal or the normality assumption is violated. The effect size is reported as rank-biserial correlation r.
:::

---

## One-way ANOVA

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "anova_one",
  question  = "Does satisfaction differ across booking channels?",
  variables = list(outcome = "satisfaction", group = "booking_channel")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   F(3, 56) = 4.21, p = .009, η² = .18
Prompt:   A one-way ANOVA indicated a statistically significant difference
          in satisfaction across booking channels, F(3, 56) = 4.21,
          p = .009, η² = .18. Post-hoc Tukey HSD revealed that...
:::

::: {.callout}
Eta-squared (η²) is the effect size. Post-hoc Tukey HSD tests are run automatically when k > 2. The writing prompt includes the post-hoc structure so you can complete it with which groups differ.
:::

---

## Kruskal-Wallis

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "kruskal_wallis",
  question  = "Does overall rating differ across visitor age groups (non-parametric)?",
  variables = list(outcome = "q_overall", group = "age_group")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   H(3) = 8.74, p = .033
Prompt:   A Kruskal-Wallis test indicated a statistically significant
          difference in overall rating across age groups,
          H(3) = 8.74, p = .033.
:::

::: {.callout}
Non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA. Use when group distributions are not approximately normal or sample sizes are small. Dunn's post-hoc test (with Bonferroni correction) is available via options.
:::

---

## Linear regression

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "regression_linear",
  question  = "Which constructs predict behavioural intention?",
  variables = list(
    outcome    = "behavioural_intention",
    predictors = c("digital_marketing", "service_quality", "satisfaction")
  )
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   F(3, 56) = 18.4, p < .001, R² = .50, adjusted R² = .47
  Predictor             β      SE     t      p
  digital_marketing    0.14   0.09   1.60   .115
  service_quality      0.22   0.10   2.23   .030  *
  satisfaction         0.41   0.09   4.48  <.001  ***
:::

::: {.callout}
Standardised coefficients (β), standard errors, t-values, p-values, and model fit indices are all returned. The writing prompt includes the full APA regression table structure.
:::

---

## Logistic regression (binary)

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "regression_logistic_binary",
  question  = "What predicts the likelihood of recommending the destination?",
  variables = list(
    outcome    = "recommend_binary",   # 0/1 coded variable
    predictors = c("satisfaction", "service_quality")
  )
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   χ²(2) = 14.3, p < .001, Nagelkerke R² = .29
  Predictor       OR     95% CI         p
  satisfaction   3.14   [1.42, 6.95]  .005  **
  service_quality 1.87   [0.94, 3.71]  .073
:::

::: {.callout}
Odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals are returned. Also available: `regression_logistic_ordinal` for ordered outcomes, `regression_logistic_multinomial` for unordered categorical outcomes.
:::

---

## Chi-square test

```r
rq <- sf_research_question(
  method    = "chi_square",
  question  = "Is booking channel associated with visitor type?",
  variables = list(row = "booking_channel", column = "visit_type")
)
```

::: {.r-out}
Result:   χ²(3) = 9.81, p = .020, V = .28
Prompt:   A chi-square test of independence indicated a statistically
          significant association between booking channel and visitor type,
          χ²(3) = 9.81, p = .020, Cramér's V = .28.
:::

::: {.callout}
Cramér's V is the effect size. When expected cell counts < 5, Fisher's exact test is used automatically and noted in the output. Use `fisher_exact` to force Fisher's test regardless.
:::

---

## {background-color="#1f6f78"}

::: {style="text-align:center; padding-top:2.8em;"}
<p class="chap-hero">CFA, SEM, and PLS-SEM syntax</p>
<p class="chap-sub">Generated from the instrument — no manual transcription</p>
:::

---

## CFA syntax — lavaan

```r
cat(cfa_lavaan_syntax(instr_d))
```

::: {.r-out}
digital_marketing     =~ dm_1 + dm_2 + dm_3
service_quality       =~ sq_1 + sq_2 + sq_3
sustainability        =~ sus_1 + sus_2
satisfaction          =~ sat_1 + sat_2
behavioural_intention =~ bi_1 + bi_2
:::

```r
# Fit the model directly
library(lavaan)
fit <- cfa(cfa_lavaan_syntax(instr_d), data = scored)
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout}
The syntax is generated from your `sf_model()` declaration. Factor names match your scale ids. Items are listed in the order they appear in the scale — no manual list needed.
:::

---

## SEM syntax — lavaan with structural paths

```r
cat(sem_lavaan_syntax(instr_d))
```

::: {.r-out}
# Measurement model
service_quality       =~ sq_1 + sq_2 + sq_3
satisfaction          =~ sat_1 + sat_2
behavioural_intention =~ bi_1 + bi_2

# Structural paths
satisfaction          ~ service_quality
behavioural_intention ~ satisfaction
:::

```r
library(lavaan)
fit_sem <- sem(sem_lavaan_syntax(instr_d), data = scored)
```

::: {.callout}
Paths are generated from the `paths` argument in `sf_model()`. Change the structural theory by editing `sf_model()` — the syntax updates automatically.
:::

---

## PLS-SEM syntax — SEMinR

```r
cat(seminr_syntax(instr_d))
```

::: {.r-out}
constructs(
  composite("digital_marketing",     multi_items("dm_",  1:3)),
  composite("service_quality",        multi_items("sq_",  1:3)),
  composite("satisfaction",           multi_items("sat_", 1:2)),
  composite("behavioural_intention",  multi_items("bi_",  1:2))
)
:::

```r
library(seminr)
mm  <- seminr_syntax(instr_d)
sm  <- relationships(paths(from = "satisfaction", to = "behavioural_intention"))
res <- estimate_pls(data = scored, measurement_model = mm, structural_model = sm)
```

::: {.callout}
`lavaan` and `seminr` are in Suggests — not required to generate the syntax. Only install them when you are ready to fit the model.
:::

## Analysis results report

```r
results <- run_analysis_plan(scored, instr_d)

render_results(
  results, instr_d,
  output_file     = "analysis_results.html",
  citation_format = "apa",
  open            = TRUE
)
```

Each research question gets its own result card containing:

- The APA result string with test statistic, df, p-value, and effect size
- The 95% confidence interval where applicable
- The statistical method and its assumptions
- A ready-to-paste writing prompt in plain academic English
- The relevant methodological citation

::: {.callout-green}
Open `analysis_results.html` in any browser. No R required to read it. Share with co-authors or paste directly into your manuscript.
:::

---

## Full study report

```r
render_report(
  instr_d,
  data                 = scored,
  output_file          = "study_report.html",
  include_codebook     = TRUE,
  include_quality      = TRUE,
  include_missing      = TRUE,
  include_descriptives = TRUE,
  include_reliability  = TRUE,
  include_analysis     = TRUE,
  open                 = TRUE
)
```

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
**Sections generated:**

- Instrument codebook (all items and scales)
- Data quality summary
- Missing data by item
- Descriptive statistics
- Scale reliability (alpha per scale)
- Analysis plan results
:::
::: {.col}
::: {.callout}
**APA table style throughout:** horizontal rules only, no vertical borders, no row shading. Tables are ready for a manuscript appendix without reformatting.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Instrument codebook

```r
render_codebook(
  instr_d,
  output_file = "codebook.html",
  open        = TRUE
)
```

The codebook documents every component of the instrument:

| Section | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Items | id, label, type, choice set, scale, required, reverse |
| Choice sets | id, values, labels |
| Scales | id, label, items, scoring method |
| Branches | item, condition, action |
| Quality checks | type, threshold, action |
| Model | factors, indicators, structural paths |

::: {.callout}
The codebook is generated entirely from the instrument object — no manual documentation needed. It updates automatically when the instrument changes.
:::

---

## Interactive response dashboard

```r
launch_dashboard_demo()
```

The dashboard opens in your browser with five tabs:

| Tab | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Overview** | Response count, date range, completion time, flagged rate |
| **Items** | Per-item frequency charts and tables |
| **Scales** | Scale score distributions with mean overlay |
| **Quality** | Attention-check pass rates with colour-coded rows |
| **Raw data** | Scrollable response table with CSV download |

::: {.callout-amber}
The dashboard is a Shiny app that runs locally — no data leaves your machine. It reads the instrument and the responses; no configuration required.
:::

## Install and run the guided demo

```r
# Install from CRAN
install.packages("surveyframe")

# Or the development version
remotes::install_github("MohammedAliSharafuddin/surveyframe")
```

```r
library(surveyframe)

# Guided walkthrough — 8 sections, ~10 minutes, fully offline
demo("survey", package = "surveyframe")

# Open the GUI builder with a pre-loaded demo instrument
launch_builder_demo()

# Full pipeline in 4 lines
d       <- sframe_demo_data()
scored  <- score_scales(d$responses, d$instrument)
results <- run_analysis_plan(scored, d$instrument)
render_results(results, d$instrument,
               output_file = tempfile(fileext = ".html"), open = TRUE)
```

---

## What makes surveyframe different

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
**surveyframe**

::: {.checklist}
- Instrument, plan, and model in one validated R object
- Analysis declared before data collection
- No post-hoc test selection
- 11 item types, 20+ analysis methods in one package
- Quality checks pre-declared, not manual
- SHA-256 hash on every `.sframe` file
- One-call APA results with writing prompts
- CFA, SEM, PLS-SEM syntax from instrument
- Fully reproducible — everything is R code
:::
:::
::: {.col}
**Other tools**

- Form builder separated from analysis tool
- Test selection after seeing data
- No machine-readable analysis contract
- Item types limited; analysis in separate software
- Quality checks done by hand
- No file integrity checking
- Manual table construction
- Syntax typed by hand from codebook
- Reproducibility depends on memory and PDFs
:::
:::
